Even when you were lost on the predecessors, they were always able to generate a flow to keep you on track. This just seemed to lack that entirely. While I regret not giving this game more of a chance, the sad reality was that perhaps I just held the expectations too high for this franchise. This just doesnt meet the standard to me, but best of luck for this team in the future."

review_text_raw:
Loved the first two games and was very excited to start the third. The prospect of a new setting---getting away from depraved online influencers and into a rural area---seemed neat. And we might even be working against a new threat, be it a new mutation of the Simulacra or perhaps a different monster altogether. 

In the previous two games, you get engaged right away.
 
Game 1 starts with the phone glitching out, emitting eerie sounds the second you touch it. Then, as though haunted, it forcibly opens one video among a dozen corrupted files, showing a brief yet shocking video that teases the main mystery: what happened to Anna and is this phone haunted? The video is fragmented and ambiguous but the victim’s distress is very clear. Her final words? “Don’t come looking for me.” Its immediately intriguing. 

In the second game you're a junior detective at the local precinct. It starts with a meeting between you and the chief, where he confides to you the existence of a secret division within the police department, one which handles unnatural phenomena. He hands you stolen evidence: a phone, from the recently deceased Maya, who's strange death frightened the PD regulars into closing her case prematurely. In light of their unwillingness to discover the truth, the chief tasks you personally with spelunking through the phone to unearth clues. He needs your help because he's an older fellow who's not technologically inclined, while you're the young whippersnapper who's hip with the youths and does the iphones. 

Right away there's a sense of urgency. The department is looking for the stolen evidence, you’re breaking the rules just by having this conversation with the chief, and this secret division desperately needs to furnish some results or risk being shut down by the higher ups. And it’s all up to you.

Like the first installment, there’s some spooky phone glitches which show us something is terribly wrong but doesn’t show us exactly what, baiting the mystery.

To help you along, the chief sets you up with cutting edge, AI based software to help you log clues, disseminate evidence, remote hack the victim’s laptop and restore corrupted files. It was developed to help law enforcement conduct investigations which, in our modern world, are increasingly linked to social technology and personal communications. So it’s at least believable. And it imparts a cool-factor, being given access to exclusive, law enforcement tech.

In game three, you’re just some indistinguishable f*ck from the neighborhood watch group. You’re met with a normal phone and some flat, uninteresting dialogue from Ruby, who decides that the best gambit to enlist your assistance is to belittle you, calling you out as the office coffee b*tch and saying “you might know me, I’m the one who’s always ordering the double tall macchiato” or whatever. As if to imply that you, you loathsome, lowly creature, are so far beneath her station that you could only recognize her by the coffees she sends you to fetch like the obedient mud worm you are.

Then, after nailing down just how useless you are, she inexplicably puts her entire case in your hands. And by “inexplicably,” I mean there’s no reason whatsoever for her to need you or trust you at all. She just heedlessly unloads her project—a project that could very easily get her fired—onto you, who she has just thoroughly disrespected.

You get another scanning tool but unlike the WARDEN app from Simulacra 2, this one feels… shoehorned. It was made by some b*tchless basement dweller named Paul, who looks and acts like a sock puppet, who’s tied his unusual app to the GPS. For reasons.

Like its predecessors, you still get to see a creepy video but its overly long and boring. And entirely too blatant. You get to see the cheesy shadow monster, what’s called “the Beldam” (a dumber name I could not fathom) without any preamble or creativity or teasing. Not only that but you stumble across it like it’s just another YouTube video in the shuffle queue. No spooky glitch, no nameless entity forcing you to look at it. Just.. “oh hey neat.”

Somehow, despite the obviousness of the monster video, when you send it to Ruby she instantly decides to go for a stroll in the very same haunted hallway, alone. Which was so unbelievably obtuse it completely shattered any immersion I’d forced myself to conjure just to make it this far.

To make matters even less interesting, everyone in town already seems to know about the Beldam. It’s on their social media, it’s in their photo reels, one @$$hole even talks about seeing its shape in his latte foam. Seriously, wtf? So there’s nothing special about you discovering its existence. Instead of engaging your morbid curiosity and imagination, it just makes you feel like you’re reading hokey bullcrap about bigfoot in a lowbrow tabloid. 

The real nail in this games’ coffin is: instead of giving us one victim to focus on, who’s distress we can directly witness and care about, we’re hit with a list of missing randos who’s peril is entirely unknown to us. They’re just “missing” y’know… kind of like the plot. 

The only threat it draws our attention to, is that a comically greedy mayor wants to pave over the local farmers market and build a mall. 
Wow. 
Call in the national guard. 
Nothing gets me quaking in my boots like the threat of a shopping mall. 

And even then, it’s just plain text. No video, no room for interpretation or imagination. They just black-and-white spell it out for you. “MaYOr bAd, mAke fARmErs sAD.”

This game completely lacks any of the inspiration and vision that made the prequels special. Feels like a cheap cash grab.

Uninstalled.

review_text_raw:
I would give a mediocre rating here, but, for me, there are more negative aspects than positive ones. If you're new to the series, I recommend skipping the first, playing the second, and forgetting about the third.

I liked Simulacra 2 very much, and that was the game I started with. Not liking the first at all, I was hoping for a more second-like game with the third. But, unfortunatelly, that's not the case.

I don't like that the developers didn't include an intro movie like in the second. Who am I? How do I get the phone? Why am I interested in having it? Of course, it is explained during the next minutes within the phone, but there's a reason that games use intro sequences since they had enough capacity to show one, and may it be only text.

Seeing the first videos on the phone, I had the feeling that the actors weren't really into the game concept, but I could live with that if there weren't the big atmosphere-killer: the ghost.

The second game focussed on the invisible threat. The third game includes CGI-monsters, and they killed every ambiance the moment I saw them. Ironically, after seeing the first CGI-ghost, you have the option to reply within a chat: "It could be fake." And of course, I clicked that answer, because it doesn't only look like fake, but it IS fake. And I got an answer from my in-game-partner that made me believe that the developers take their CGI-ghosts seriously: "No, the video isn't edited".

As with every computer generated horror within a movie, it looks artificial and restricts the atmosphere. I always know I'm watching a movie only.

With that in mind, clicking through the webpages, chats, and media, solving sometimes too easy, sometimes nonsense-riddles, feels unsatisfying, because all you will come to see is more of the CGI-illusion. *Spoiler* The ghost's hands in the office - they took away the thrill instantly! *Spoiler end*

I think, there was a peak with the second game that cannot be repeated so easily.

review_text_raw:
Even with only 3 hours this game feels like it drags on forever. New characters are introduced way late into the game so you don't give a crap about them, and the ones they do use are just one dimensional exposition dumps with nothing interesting behind them. Unlocking new information on the phone wasn't rewarding, and some of the puzzles were way too tedious, looking for a single spec of information in a sea of nothing. I played this with a group and we were all angry when we figured out a puzzle, they just don't work.

Worst part is, this fails as a horror game as well. The scawy ghost is shown to you constantly so there's no fear of the unknown. The repetition of the symbol isn't scary, it's just goofy. The best part of the game is when the background freaked out and that was the only thing with any interest. It lasts a whole 15 seconds. Every video is just a nothing burger with the person 'seeing something in the distance.' Think paranormal activity 2 levels of boring surveillance. 

It fails at horror, fails at a compelling story, no interesting character, and no fun puzzles. It's just nothing. Just play the other 2 games. They ain't perfect, but better than this by a landslide.

review_text_raw:
I just finished my first play through of the game and got what I can assume is the expected good ending. Given the gallery, there seems to be multiple types of endings.

This was... short. Much shorter than 2.

I have about 15 hours in Simulacra 2 while this took 3 hours to finish.

That being said, this was because the puzzles and sleuthing required in Simulacra 2 was more obscure and multiparted than what is presented in 3. The to do list was more hints and solutions than just minor quests this time around as it was more specific and broken into far more steps for greater clarity. This made the game much faster to go through as you almost always knew what to do next and could get huge help from the people you were speaking with. Perhaps this was feedback from how 2 was too obscure and some people felt like they spent hours looking for something entirely not obvious to them so this was added to help with it.

I can see it helping but it made it feel like I really wasnt needed. All these people had literally the answers themselves and all i had was someones phone. Any one else could have figured it out where as in 2 I felt like only I COULD solve it.

The feed has been streamlined and what you unlock instead is barfed at you in large chunks instead of the steady trickle that you get from social media sleuthing like in 2. This however made everything feel less personal. I didnt care about the missing people at all since they had nothing else going for them identity wise. They were footnotes pushed in to move the story along.

There doesnt seem to be a lot of character in this one. Pacing with the characters seem incredibly jarring as you go from casual work associates to suddenly having to answer deep mental health trauma in scenarios that come from left field and not in a natural way. The social media aspects were very lacking as you couldnt explore much except a small town feed.

Its easy to describe a story as 4 acts. The hook, the crescendo, the reveal, then the resolution.

I didnt feel like there was a lot of build up. The hook is the crescendo itself. Going into game knowing people are missing already was not really that interesting. Before I knew it, I found myself collecting pieces to finish the "ritual" to solve the problem. This also did not feel like I was apart of the story or had much agency. All the pieces were given to me because i asked someone nicely. A relationship that was already built by someone I never meet. I take advantage of all his work, his relationships, and his findings, just to ask other people to do the big bits for me. I never perform any of the rituals, I never do any of the fighting, I am way more of a casual observer than someone who held anyone's fate in my hands.

The ending left me really bored as I truly didnt feel what the relationship was between any of the people. The premise is a bit wonky as its a shut in PI type that just made esoteric relationships with various people around town that suddenly become holders of big puzzle pieces.

I am guessing due to pandemic, the development had to cut back because there doesnt seem to be a giant web of possibilities like 2 did, there are very straight cut and dry of live or die decisions and I kept feeling like I could have messed up everything when the wording between two dialogue options were basically the same and you had only 3 seconds to choose.

Some of the UI and UX were confusing. The minigame felt incredibly easy but that made me question if I was getting baited into something but instead it really was just simply as it was presented. It was more tedious than fun because you had to watch some really weird forced acting as you played the truck guy in phasmophobia on a far smaller scale essentially. 

Not as good as 2. Still recommend because it was enjoyable but definitely a weaker production in comparison.

review_text_raw: In the context of the rest of the series, this game feels lazy and rushed. The scenes featuring choices have horrible CG—while the previous games in the series didn't have great CG, it was at least passable; here, it's downright terrible. There are also awkward, jarring cuts after selecting choices during some character dialogue scenes. The ending is particularly disappointing, as it simply dumps exposition in text rather than showcasing the events through actual filmed or designed sequences like the first two games did. Overall, I’d recommend skipping this one. While the story itself isn’t bad, the execution is lacking in almost every way.

(This is more of a mixed review than a good one but steam doesn't give an option for that so yeah).

[b]The story[/b] of simulacra 3 was actually pretty good but it's a massively slow burner and doesn't FEEL like a simulacra story, for example, [spoiler] the main antagonist has nothing to do with technology where as the other games all had the simulacrums interacting with social media, dating apps and Mobile games, where as the villain of simulacra 3, 'the Beldam' is basically just a standard ghost story ghost, with the simulacra label attached to it. [/spoiler].

[b]The gameplay[/b] itself is standard simulacra gameplay with a few sections that are slightly different, I have no complaints about this other than more of the CCTV sections would've been nice.

[b]The Characters[/b] in this one, sorta just exist and I didn't like any of them, even ones we where supposed to like.

[b]The horror[/b] in simulacra  3 is a lot more toned down, I think this has been a problem with every entry since the first one, none of them have been as scary as that first game. I will say though the ambient sounds in this one are actually scary and got me a few times.

[b]Overall[/b], I think if you're like me and you loved the other simulacra games, you'll like this one. The game has it's faults but there's a decent story and some decent mysteries in there, but maybe play one of the other ones if you're gonna choose one simulacra game to play.
